## Overview

This appendix documents the procedure used to determine which predictors enter the multi-scale habitat association models. Two screening steps set the budget: (1) an events-per-parameter (EPP) analysis, which constrains the number of fixed-effect habitat predictors to a level supportable by the number of non-zero detection events in the most data-limited temporal period, and (2) variance inflation factor (VIF) screening across all 16 spatial extents, confirming that collinearity among candidate predictors does not further reduce the budget. A third section documents (3) the predictor selection procedure that fills the budget. All analyses use the negative binomial GLM framework described in the main text.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(car)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))

# ── Constants ──
month_levels <- c("May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "October")
focal_species <- c("Horse", "Cattle", "Elk")
dredge_covars <- c("p_herb", "p_shrub", "p_harvest", "p_wetland", "hu", "tri")

covar_colors <- c(
  "p_harvest" = "#E69F00", "p_herb" = "#90C060",
  "p_shrub" = "#9467BD", "p_wetland" = "#5B9BD5",
  "hu" = "#C44E52", "tri" = "#8B5A2B"
)

# ── Temporal structures ──
horse_months <- 5:10
cattle_bimonthly <- list("Jul-Aug" = c(7, 8), "Sep-Oct" = c(9, 10))
elk_quarterly <- list("May-Jul" = c(5, 6, 7), "Aug-Oct" = c(8, 9, 10))
```

```{r load-data}
dat_raw <- read_csv("input/analysis_ready_multiscale.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(
    month_name = factor(month_name, levels = month_levels),
    strata = factor(strata, levels = c("Open", "Forest", "Harvest", "Linear", "Riparian")),
    species = factor(species, levels = focal_species),
    NDVI_herb = replace_na(NDVI_herb, 0)
  )

all_scales <- sort(unique(dat_raw$extent_radius_m))
ref_scale <- all_scales[1]

# Drop rows with NA hu
dat <- dat_raw %>% filter(!is.na(hu))
```

```{r pooled-datasets}
# ── Create pooled datasets for cattle (bimonthly) and elk (quarterly) ──
pool_months <- function(data, month_vec, period_label) {
  data %>%
    filter(month %in% month_vec) %>%
    group_by(location, species, year, extent_radius_m, strata, strata_code,
             latitude, longitude) %>%
    summarise(
      n_det = sum(n_det), camera_days = sum(camera_days),
      p_herb = first(p_herb), p_shrub = first(p_shrub),
      p_wetland = first(p_wetland), p_harvest = first(p_harvest),
      tri = first(tri), NDVI_herb = mean(NDVI_herb, na.rm = TRUE),
      hu = mean(hu, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(log_effort = log(camera_days), period = period_label,
           strata = factor(strata, levels = c("Open", "Forest", "Harvest", "Linear", "Riparian"))) %>%
    filter(camera_days >= 7)
}

cattle_bimonthly_data <- map2_dfr(
  cattle_bimonthly, names(cattle_bimonthly),
  ~ pool_months(filter(dat, species == "Cattle"), .x, .y)
)

elk_quarterly_data <- map2_dfr(
  elk_quarterly, names(elk_quarterly),
  ~ pool_months(filter(dat, species == "Elk"), .x, .y)
)
```

## Events-Per-Parameter (EPP) Analysis

The predictor budget is constrained by the number of non-zero detection events in the most limiting temporal period. Following the adaptation of Harrell's (2015) rule for count models, we require a minimum of 10 non-zero events per estimated parameter, counting only fixed-effect habitat predictors and the spatial autocovariate (SAC) against the budget:

$$k_{\text{max}} = \left\lfloor \frac{n_{\text{non-zero}}}{10} \right\rfloor - 1$$

where the subtracted 1 accounts for the SAC.

Events are defined as camera-months with at least one detection, on the reasoning that in these zero-heavy count distributions the non-zero observations are the primary source of information for estimating predictor effects. The guideline was developed for binary outcomes and its applicability to negative binomial count models has not been formally evaluated, so we apply it as a conservative constraint on model complexity rather than as a validated criterion.

Habitat stratum is not counted against these budgets. It is a design blocking factor fitted in every model rather than a candidate predictor, and the stratum contrasts are reported in Supporting Information S7 rather than treated as competing terms.

```{r epp-analysis}
# Horse: monthly
horse_epp <- dat %>%
  filter(species == "Horse", extent_radius_m == ref_scale) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs = n(), n_nonzero = sum(n_det > 0),
    pct_zero = round(100 * mean(n_det == 0), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(species = "Horse", period = month.abb[month],
         max_k_habitat = pmax(0, floor(n_nonzero / 10) - 1))

# Cattle: bimonthly
cattle_epp <- cattle_bimonthly_data %>%
  filter(extent_radius_m == ref_scale) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs = n(), n_nonzero = sum(n_det > 0),
    pct_zero = round(100 * mean(n_det == 0), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(species = "Cattle", max_k_habitat = pmax(0, floor(n_nonzero / 10) - 1))

# Elk: quarterly
elk_epp <- elk_quarterly_data %>%
  filter(extent_radius_m == ref_scale) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs = n(), n_nonzero = sum(n_det > 0),
    pct_zero = round(100 * mean(n_det == 0), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(species = "Elk", max_k_habitat = pmax(0, floor(n_nonzero / 10) - 1))

epp_all <- bind_rows(horse_epp, cattle_epp, elk_epp) %>%
  select(species, period, n_obs, n_nonzero, pct_zero, max_k_habitat)

kable(epp_all,
      caption = "EPP analysis: maximum habitat predictors per species-period. Budget overhead = SAC (1 parameter).",
      col.names = c("Species", "Period", "N obs", "N non-zero", "% zero",
                     "Max habitat predictors")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

Because predictors are held constant across temporal periods within each species (i.e., the same set of habitat predictors is used in every monthly or pooled-period model), the predictor budget is set by the most limiting period:

```{r uniform-budget}
budget_summary <- epp_all %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    limiting_period = period[which.min(max_k_habitat)],
    min_nonzero = min(n_nonzero),
    uniform_max_k = min(max_k_habitat),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(budget_summary,
      caption = "Uniform predictor budget per species, constrained by the most limiting temporal period.",
      col.names = c("Species", "Limiting period", "Min N non-zero", "Max habitat predictors")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

## Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Screening

Because the multi-scale analysis fits models at 16 spatial extents ranging from 40 m to 7.2 km, collinearity among landscape composition predictors could vary with scale, buffer compositions tend to converge toward regional means at broad extents. VIF was therefore computed for all six candidate predictors at every species × temporal period × spatial extent combination. A conventional threshold of VIF < 5 was used to flag problematic collinearity.

```{r vif-function}
# Compute VIF per species × period × scale using car::vif() on a linear model
compute_vif_at_scale <- function(data, covars, scale_m) {
  d <- data %>% filter(extent_radius_m == scale_m)
  if (nrow(d) < length(covars) + 2) return(NULL)
  for (v in covars) d[[v]] <- as.numeric(scale(d[[v]]))
  form <- as.formula(paste0("n_det ~ ", paste(covars, collapse = " + ")))
  tryCatch({
    vif_vals <- car::vif(lm(form, data = d))
    tibble(covariate = names(vif_vals), vif = as.numeric(vif_vals), extent_radius_m = scale_m)
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
}
```

```{r vif-compute}
# Horse: VIF at each month × scale
horse_vif <- map_dfr(horse_months, function(m) {
  d <- dat %>% filter(species == "Horse", month == m)
  map_dfr(all_scales, ~ compute_vif_at_scale(d, dredge_covars, .x)) %>%
    mutate(period = month.abb[m], species = "Horse")
})

# Cattle: VIF at each bimonthly period × scale
cattle_vif <- map_dfr(names(cattle_bimonthly), function(p) {
  d <- cattle_bimonthly_data %>% filter(period == p)
  map_dfr(all_scales, ~ compute_vif_at_scale(d, dredge_covars, .x)) %>%
    mutate(period = p, species = "Cattle")
})

# Elk: VIF at each quarterly period × scale
elk_vif <- map_dfr(names(elk_quarterly), function(p) {
  d <- elk_quarterly_data %>% filter(period == p)
  map_dfr(all_scales, ~ compute_vif_at_scale(d, dredge_covars, .x)) %>%
    mutate(period = p, species = "Elk")
})

all_vif <- bind_rows(horse_vif, cattle_vif, elk_vif)

# Summarise: maximum VIF across all temporal periods, per species × scale × predictor
vif_max <- all_vif %>%
  group_by(species, extent_radius_m, covariate) %>%
  summarise(max_vif = max(vif, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r vif-plot, fig.height=7, fig.cap="**Figure S3.1.** Variance inflation factors (VIF) for the six candidate habitat predictors across 16 spatial extents, by species. Values shown are the maximum VIF across all temporal periods within each species. Red dashed line marks the conventional VIF = 5 threshold; red dotted line marks VIF = 10. All predictors remain below VIF = 5 at all scales for all species."}
ggplot(vif_max, aes(x = extent_radius_m, y = max_vif, color = covariate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dotted", color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = function(x) ifelse(x < 1000, paste0(x, "m"),
                                              paste0(round(x/1000, 1), "km"))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = covar_colors[names(covar_colors) %in% dredge_covars]) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Buffer radius", y = "VIF", color = "Predictor"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

VIF remains below 5 at all spatial extents for all species. The modest upward trend at broad scales (p_wetland approaching ~4.0 and p_herb ~3.5 at 7.2 km for horses) is expected as buffer compositions converge toward regional means. Because only four of the Hermosilla et al. (2018, 2022) landcover classes are included as predictors, the remaining classes (forest, barren, water, etc.) absorb the compositional constraint, proportions do not sum to 1 among the included predictors, and VIF confirms no practical collinearity problem. No predictors require exclusion on collinearity grounds at any spatial extent.

## Predictor Selection

The base predictor set for each species was identified by fitting every combination of predictors at the species' budget size, drawn from six eligible predictors (proportion herbaceous, proportion shrub, proportion harvest, proportion wetland, human use and TRI), at each of the 16 spatial extents. For each fitted model we computed AIC and derived Akaike weights within each extent. We then calculated cumulative variable importance as the sum of Akaike weights across all models containing a given predictor, aggregated across extents and temporal periods, and retained the highest-scoring predictors up to the species' budget.

The seventh predictor, herbaceous NDVI, was excluded from this screening. Herbaceous NDVI carries structural NA values wherever proportion herbaceous is zero, and these are imputed to zero. Screened on its own, the imputed zeros would attenuate its estimated effect, because nothing else in the model would distinguish a location with no herbaceous cover from a location with herbaceous cover and low greenness. Proportion herbaceous makes that distinction, so herbaceous NDVI is interpretable only when the two are fitted together, and it was handled exclusively through the substitution procedure described in the main text.

The relationship between herbaceous NDVI and proportion herbaceous is additive. An interaction term is unnecessary because imputing NDVI to zero wherever proportion herbaceous is zero already encodes the structural dependency between them.

All predictors within a model were measured at the same spatial extent, a matched-scale design. Scale of effect estimates are therefore conditional on the other predictors being measured at the same extent, and the true optimal scale for an individual predictor could differ under a mixed-scale design.

## Final Predictor Budgets

```{r budget-final}
budget_final <- budget_summary %>%
  transmute(
    Species               = species,
    `EPP limit`           = uniform_max_k,
    `Limiting period`     = limiting_period,
    `Limiting N non-zero` = min_nonzero
  ) %>%
  # Join by name rather than assuming row order: summarise() returns
  # budget_summary alphabetically (Cattle, Elk, Horse).
  left_join(
    tibble(
      Species              = c("Horse", "Cattle", "Elk"),
      `Temporal structure` = c("Monthly (May–Oct)",
                               "Bimonthly (Jul–Aug, Sep–Oct)",
                               "Quarterly (May–Jul, Aug–Oct)")
    ),
    by = "Species"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(Species, `EPP limit`, `Temporal structure`,
                `Limiting period`, `Limiting N non-zero`) %>%
  arrange(factor(Species, levels = c("Horse", "Cattle", "Elk")))

kable(budget_final,
      caption = "Final predictor budget and temporal structure for each species.") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

The species-specific temporal pooling structures reflect differences in detection frequency and seasonal presence. Horses are detected sufficiently often to support monthly models; cattle and elk require bimonthly and quarterly pooling, respectively, to achieve adequate non-zero events. Elk are the most data-limited species, with only 36 non-zero quarterly events in the Aug–Oct period constraining the budget to two habitat predictors plus the SAC. VIF remains below 5 at all spatial extents for all species (Figure S3.1), confirming that collinearity among the candidate predictors does not impose additional constraints beyond the EPP limit.
